newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich vows to expand Medicare benefits.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich vows to expand Medicare benefits.

text.p: U.S. House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich on Thursday threw his support behind a bill to expand preventive benefits under Medicare, saying his mother-in-law's battle with diabetes had shown him the need for such aid.

In rare testimony before the House Ways and Means Committee, Gingrich endorsed a bipartisan bill requiring Medicare to cover mammograms, prostate cancer and colorectal cancer screening as well as self-management training and routine blood tests for diabetics.
President Bill Clinton has proposed a similar expansion of Medicare benefits as part of his balanced budget plan.

"There is a dramatic difference in what happens to someone with diabetes if they do take care of themselves or if they don't," Gingrich told the committee, saying he wanted to ensure the bill passed "with a huge bipartisan majority."
The Georgia Republican told of watching his mother-in-law Virginia Ginther, a long-time diabetic, struggle to control the disease.

Advocates of the legislation, introduced by California Republican Bill Thomas and Maryland Democrat Ben Cardin, said early detection and proper care could prevent some serious health problems associated with diabetes, such as blindness, kidney failure, amputation and heart disease.

About 9 percent of the Medicare population has been diagnosed with diabetes. But about $28.6 billion a year, or nearly 30 percent of the Medicare budget, is spent on care for diabetics. Nationally 16 million people are believed to have diabetes, but about half have not been diagnosed.
Gingrich criticised the Congressional Budget Office, which says preventive services would increase Medicare spending. Aides said the bill could cost $3.5 billion over five years.
Republicans have warned Medicare is quickly going broke. Unless the legislation is brought up as part of a balanced budget deal, new spending could be a problem.
Gingrich said detection and care would save money, saying the CBO was "simply wrong. It is archaic, it is antihuman."

Congressional Budget Office analysts said preventive care could increase health costs for many reasons. For example, a large number of people might receive screening and followup tests though only a relatively few turn out to be ill.

The bill would provide coverage for annual mammograms for women over age 49; increase coverage for pelvic exams and provide for annual colorectal and prostate screening for those over 50. It would cover diabetes screening including self-management training services and blood-testing strips.

Other lawmakers appeared before the committee to offer testimonials. Virginia Democrat Norm Sisisky told of his fight with colorectal cancer. Washington Republican George Nethercutt and Oregon Democrat Elizabeth Furse spoke of their experiences as parents of children with diabetes.
